title: Matplotlib Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Matplotlib lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Figures and axes
entries.summary: A figure is the whole chart image. An Axes object is an area inside it where data is drawn.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 3])
plt.show()

notes: Matplotlib uses Axes as an object name; it is different from one single x or y axis.

entries.name: Label the meaning
entries.summary: Axis labels explain what values mean and which units they use. A title tells the reader the chart's topic.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 3])
ax.set_xlabel("Day")
ax.set_ylabel("Books read")
ax.set_title("Reading this week")
plt.show()

notes: A chart without units can be misleading even if its points are correct.

entries.name: Compare categories with bars
entries.summary: A bar chart compares categories. Bars usually start from zero so their lengths fairly represent the values.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["Art", "Music", "Sport"], [3, 5, 4])
ax.set_ylabel("Votes")
plt.show()

notes: Cutting off the zero baseline can exaggerate bar differences.

entries.name: Use a scatter plot for pairs
entries.summary: A scatter plot shows paired measurements as separate points. It helps reveal a relationship without connecting every point.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter([1, 2, 3], [4, 3, 5])
ax.set_xlabel("Practice sessions")
ax.set_ylabel("Points")
plt.show()

notes: Do not claim causation from a simple visual relationship.

entries.name: Histograms group numeric values
entries.summary: A histogram groups numbers into bins and counts how many fall in each bin. A bin is an interval, not a category label.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist([1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3], bins=[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5])
ax.set_xlabel("Books per learner")
ax.set_ylabel("Learners")
plt.show()

notes: Changing bin widths changes the appearance of a histogram.

entries.name: Legends identify series
entries.summary: A legend matches a line or marker to its label. It is useful when one chart has more than one series.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2], [2, 3], label="Red team")
ax.plot([1, 2], [3, 4], label="Blue team")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

notes: Do not rely on color alone to distinguish important series.

entries.name: Control visible limits carefully
entries.summary: Axis limits choose the part of the number range shown. Use them deliberately and tell readers when a narrow range matters.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [8, 9, 10])
ax.set_ylim(0, 12)
plt.show()

notes: A zoomed axis can make a small difference look huge.

entries.name: Place two plots in one figure
entries.summary: subplots can create several plotting areas. Give each area clear labels so readers can compare them correctly.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)
axes[0].bar(["A", "B"], [2, 3])
axes[1].plot([1, 2], [3, 4])
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

notes: Do not assume panels have identical scales unless you set or share them.

entries.name: Grid lines support reading
entries.summary: A light grid can help readers estimate values. It should support the data rather than overpower it.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 3])
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.show()

notes: Too many heavy lines make a chart harder to read.

entries.name: Save a figure to a file
entries.summary: savefig writes the figure to a file. Choose a format and size appropriate for how it will be used.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["Books", "Pens"], [2, 3])
fig.savefig("practice-chart.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.close(fig)

notes: Save the intended figure explicitly when several figures are open.

entries.name: Explain missing observations
entries.summary: Missing data should not be silently shown as a real zero. A gap can honestly show that no observation was recorded.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3], [2, float("nan"), 4], marker="o")
plt.show()

notes: Filling missing data requires a justified choice, not a convenient visual shortcut.

entries.name: Review the story the chart tells
entries.summary: A chart should answer a clear question without exaggerating. Check title, units, scale and the underlying values before sharing.

example.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(["Monday", "Tuesday"], [4, 5])
ax.set_ylabel("Books borrowed")
ax.set_title("Fictional library example")
ax.set_ylim(0, 6)
plt.show()

notes: Do not present practice numbers as collected real-world evidence.
